directAnswer: Pope Alexander VIII was Pietro Ottoboni, a Venetian nobleman and veteran canon lawyer who was elected at about 79 and reigned from 6 October 1689 to 1 February 1691. In his brief pontificate he condemned the theory of 'philosophical sin,' censured Jansenist propositions, and formally rejected the Gallican Articles of 1682.

sections.h2: A Venetian Jurist in the Roman Curia
paras: Pietro Ottoboni was born in Venice in 1610 to a family of the Venetian patriciate and trained in law at the University of Padua. He spent decades in Rome as a judge of the Roman Rota, the Church's high appellate court, and was made a cardinal in 1652 under Innocent X. Later he served as bishop of Brescia and held senior posts in the Curia, so by the time of the 1689 conclave he was among the most experienced churchmen in the city.

His election followed the death of Innocent XI, a reforming and austere pope. Ottoboni's advanced age made him an acceptable compromise, and the French crown, whose relations with Rome had become badly strained, regarded him as more conciliatory than his predecessor.

sections.h2: Philosophical Sin, Jansenism and the Gallican Articles
paras: Alexander VIII's most lasting acts were doctrinal. In 1690 the Holy Office under his authority condemned the thesis of 'philosophical sin,' the claim that a person who does not know God, or does not think of God when acting, commits only an offense against reason and not a grave sin against God. The idea had been defended in a Jesuit college in France, and its condemnation affirmed that the moral law is always rooted in God.

The same year he condemned a list of propositions associated with Jansenism, the rigorist movement that troubled French Catholicism throughout the seventeenth century. He also signed the constitution Inter multiplices, which declared null the Four Gallican Articles adopted by the French clergy in 1682. Those articles had sought to limit papal authority in France, and Alexander's ruling kept the question open until his successor reached a settlement with Louis XIV.

sections.h2: Nepotism, Venice and the Vatican Library
paras: Alexander VIII is often criticized for reviving the favoritism toward relatives that Innocent XI had resisted. He named his grandnephew, also called Pietro Ottoboni, a cardinal while still a young man, and other family members received lucrative offices. The younger Cardinal Ottoboni later became one of Rome's great patrons of music.

As a Venetian, the pope supported his native republic in its war against the Ottoman Empire with financial subsidies. He also enriched the Vatican Library by acquiring a large part of the manuscript collection of Queen Christina of Sweden, the convert who had lived in Rome until her death in 1689. In 1690 he presided over the canonization of several saints, among them John of God and Paschal Baylon. He died in February 1691 and is buried in St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Pietro Ottoboni in Venice in 1610
Reigned 6 October 1689 – 1 February 1691
Condemned the thesis of 'philosophical sin' in 1690
Declared the Gallican Articles of 1682 null in Inter multiplices
Acquired much of Queen Christina of Sweden's manuscript library for the Vatican
Buried in St. Peter's Basilica

faqs.question: What was the 'philosophical sin' Pope Alexander VIII condemned?
faqs.answer: It was the theory that someone who acts without knowledge or thought of God commits only a 'philosophical' fault against reason rather than a true sin against God. Alexander VIII's Holy Office rejected it in 1690, holding that grave moral wrongs offend God regardless.

faqs.question: Why is Alexander VIII associated with nepotism?
faqs.answer: After the strict Innocent XI, Alexander VIII again gave cardinal's rank and profitable offices to relatives, most notably his grandnephew Pietro Ottoboni. Historians usually count this as the chief weakness of his short reign.

faqs.question: How did Alexander VIII respond to Gallicanism?
faqs.answer: He signed the constitution Inter multiplices declaring the 1682 Gallican Articles of the French clergy null and void, reaffirming papal authority against attempts to restrict it in France.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent XII was Antonio Pignatelli, a Neapolitan nobleman who reigned from 12 July 1691 to 27 September 1700. He is best remembered for the 1692 bull Romanum decet Pontificem, which sharply restricted papal nepotism, and for ending the long dispute with Louis XIV over the Gallican Articles.

sections.h2: From Papal Diplomat to Archbishop of Naples
paras: Antonio Pignatelli was born in 1615 at Spinazzola in the Kingdom of Naples, into one of the old aristocratic families of southern Italy. He entered the papal service young and built his career in diplomacy, serving as nuncio in Tuscany, Poland and Vienna. Innocent XI made him a cardinal in 1681 and appointed him archbishop of Naples, a great see he governed until his election.

The conclave of 1691 lasted about five months, divided between French, Spanish and imperial interests. Pignatelli emerged as a candidate of integrity, and he took the name Innocent in honor of Innocent XI, whose reforming spirit he intended to continue.

sections.h2: Romanum decet Pontificem and the End of the Cardinal-Nephew
paras: In 1692 Innocent XII issued Romanum decet Pontificem, a bull that forbade popes to enrich their relatives with estates, offices or revenues. It allowed at most one qualified relative to be made a cardinal and limited what such a relative could receive. The bull effectively ended the office of the cardinal-nephew, a powerful position that had shaped papal government since the Middle Ages, and later cardinals were required to swear to observe it.

The reform had practical effects on papal finances. Innocent also curbed the sale of offices in the Curia and tried to make the administration of justice in Rome more orderly, gathering the city's tribunals in a large building on the Piazza di Montecitorio, which later became the seat of the Italian Chamber of Deputies.

sections.h2: Settling Gallicanism and Judging Fénelon
paras: Relations with France had been tense since the French clergy's Declaration of 1682. Under Innocent XII a compromise was reached in 1693: Louis XIV withdrew the requirement that the Gallican Articles be taught, and French bishops who had taken part in the assembly wrote letters of regret to the pope, after which Rome confirmed new French bishops who had long been left without canonical approval.

Late in his reign Innocent was drawn into the controversy between two great French bishops, Bossuet and Fénelon, over Quietism and the nature of pure love of God. In 1699 the pope condemned a set of propositions from Fénelon's Maxims of the Saints, though in measured terms. Fénelon submitted publicly, an act widely admired at the time.

sections.h2: Charity in Rome and the Jubilee of 1700
paras: Innocent XII liked to call the poor his nephews, a phrase that summed up his intent to redirect resources from family to charity. He expanded the Hospice of San Michele as a home for orphans, the elderly and the destitute, and supported other charitable and educational foundations in Rome.
He opened the Jubilee Year of 1700 but was already seriously ill and could not preside over most of its ceremonies. He died in September 1700, and his monument stands in St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Antonio Pignatelli at Spinazzola, Kingdom of Naples, in 1615
Reigned 12 July 1691 – 27 September 1700
Issued Romanum decet Pontificem (1692) restricting nepotism
Reached a 1693 settlement with Louis XIV on the Gallican Articles
Condemned propositions from Fénelon's Maxims of the Saints in 1699
Opened the Jubilee Year of 1700

faqs.question: What did Romanum decet Pontificem do?
faqs.answer: This 1692 bull of Innocent XII barred popes from giving estates, offices and revenues to relatives and limited the number of relatives who could be made cardinals. It effectively abolished the influential office of the cardinal-nephew.

faqs.question: What was Innocent XII's role in the Fénelon controversy?
faqs.answer: In 1699 he condemned a number of propositions from Archbishop Fénelon's book on spirituality, Maxims of the Saints, which critics linked to Quietism. Fénelon accepted the judgment and submitted.

faqs.question: Why did Innocent XII call the poor his nephews?
faqs.answer: The saying expressed his policy of ending papal favoritism toward family members and directing Church resources instead to charitable works such as the Hospice of San Michele in Rome.

directAnswer: Pope Clement XI was Giovanni Francesco Albani of Urbino, who reigned from 23 November 1700 to 19 March 1721, one of the longer pontificates of the era. He issued the bull Unigenitus against Jansenism, ruled against the Chinese Rites, made the feast of the Immaculate Conception a holy day for the whole Church, and steered the papacy through the War of the Spanish Succession.

sections.h2: A Reluctant Pope Elected at Fifty-One
paras: Giovanni Francesco Albani was born in Urbino in 1649 and was known as a gifted Latinist and scholar. He held a series of Curial posts, was made a cardinal in 1690, and became an influential drafter of papal documents. Notably, he had been ordained a priest only shortly before the conclave of 1700.

Elected at fifty-one, young by the standards of the time, Albani reportedly hesitated for days before accepting. His reign began just as the death of the childless Charles II of Spain set off a struggle among the European powers for the Spanish throne.

sections.h2: Unigenitus and the Jansenist Crisis
paras: Jansenism, with its stern views of grace and its resistance to Roman authority, remained a source of division in France. In 1705 Clement XI issued Vineam Domini, which rejected the Jansenist tactic of 'respectful silence' toward earlier condemnations. In 1713 he issued the constitution Unigenitus, condemning 101 propositions from the Moral Reflections on the New Testament by Pasquier Quesnel.

Unigenitus became one of the most contested papal documents of the eighteenth century. A group of French bishops and clergy appealed against it to a future general council, and the controversy over its acceptance shaped French Church life for decades after Clement's death.

sections.h2: The Chinese Rites Decision
paras: Jesuit missionaries in China had allowed converts to keep certain ceremonies honoring Confucius and ancestors, judging them civil rather than religious. Other missionaries disagreed. After long investigation, Clement XI approved a decree in 1704 forbidding the practices, sent a legate, Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon, to China, and in 1715 issued the bull Ex illa die requiring missionaries to swear obedience to the ruling.

The decision provoked opposition from the Kangxi Emperor and seriously hindered missionary work in China. The question was settled definitively only in the twentieth century, when Pius XII in 1939 permitted Chinese Catholics to take part in such civil ceremonies.

sections.h2: War, Devotion and Learning
paras: During the War of the Spanish Succession the Papal States were caught between the Bourbon and Habsburg camps. Imperial troops occupied papal territory, including Comacchio, and Clement was forced in 1709 to recognize the Habsburg claimant Charles as king of Spain, angering the Bourbons. The Peace of Utrecht later disposed of Italian lands with little regard for papal claims.

Clement XI's devotional legacy endures. In 1708 he extended the feast of the Immaculate Conception on December 8 to the universal Church as a holy day of obligation, and after the Christian victory over the Ottomans at Petrovaradin in 1716 he extended the feast of the Holy Rosary to the whole Church. He also sent scholars to collect Eastern manuscripts for the Vatican Library and encouraged study of Rome's Christian antiquities.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Francesco Albani in Urbino in 1649
Reigned 23 November 1700 – 19 March 1721
Issued Unigenitus (1713) condemning 101 propositions of Quesnel
Ruled against the Chinese Rites, confirmed in Ex illa die (1715)
Made the Immaculate Conception (December 8) a universal feast in 1708
Extended the feast of the Holy Rosary to the universal Church in 1716

faqs.question: What was the bull Unigenitus?
faqs.answer: Unigenitus, issued by Clement XI in 1713, condemned 101 propositions from Pasquier Quesnel's Jansenist-leaning commentary on the New Testament. It caused prolonged controversy in France, where some clergy appealed against it.

faqs.question: Why did Clement XI forbid the Chinese Rites?
faqs.answer: After long study he concluded that ceremonies honoring Confucius and ancestors, as then practiced, were incompatible with Christian worship. His rulings of 1704 and 1715 were relaxed only in 1939 under Pius XII.

faqs.question: What did Clement XI do for the feast of the Immaculate Conception?
faqs.answer: In 1708 he extended the December 8 feast of the Immaculate Conception to the entire Church as a holy day of obligation, nearly 150 years before Pius IX defined the doctrine as dogma.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent XIII was Michelangelo dei Conti, a Roman nobleman and former nuncio to Portugal who reigned from 8 May 1721 to 7 March 1724. His short pontificate, hampered by poor health, was marked by pressure on the Jesuits over the Chinese Rites, a reform bull for the Church in Spain, and diplomacy with the Habsburg emperor.

sections.h2: Heir of a Papal Family
paras: Michelangelo dei Conti was born in 1655 at Poli, near Rome, into the Conti family, which had already given the Church several popes, including Innocent III in the thirteenth century. He chose the name Innocent partly in memory of that famous ancestor.

He served as a governor in the Papal States and then spent years as nuncio in Switzerland and in Portugal, where he became well acquainted with the politics of the Iberian courts. Clement XI made him a cardinal in 1706, and he later served as bishop of Viterbo before ill health led him to resign the see.

sections.h2: The Jesuits and the Chinese Rites
paras: Innocent XIII inherited the bitter dispute over the Chinese Rites, which his predecessor had forbidden. Reports reached Rome that some Jesuit missionaries were slow to comply. Innocent took a firm line, demanding obedience from the Society's superiors and, according to standard accounts, threatening to bar the order from receiving new members until compliance was assured. He died before the matter came to a resolution.
His approach reflected a wider concern in Rome about the independence of the great religious orders in mission lands, a tension that would grow throughout the eighteenth century.

sections.h2: Apostolici Ministerii and Diplomacy with the Powers
paras: In the bull Apostolici ministerii Innocent XIII addressed the Church in Spain, seeking to restore clerical discipline, regulate ordinations, and improve the formation and conduct of the clergy. Its provisions also bore on Spain's territories overseas.

In politics he sought peace with the Habsburg Emperor Charles VI and granted him investiture of the Kingdom of Naples, although the dispute over the duchies of Parma and Piacenza remained unresolved. Like his predecessor, he supported the exiled Catholic Stuart claimant James Francis Edward Stuart, who lived in Rome. Innocent XIII suffered from chronic illness throughout his reign and died in March 1724 after less than three years as pope.

keyFacts: Born Michelangelo dei Conti at Poli, near Rome, in 1655
Reigned 8 May 1721 – 7 March 1724
From the Conti family, which also produced Innocent III
Former nuncio to Switzerland and Portugal
Issued the bull Apostolici ministerii on Church discipline in Spain

faqs.question: Was Innocent XIII related to Innocent III?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both belonged to the Conti family of Latium, which had produced several medieval popes. Michelangelo dei Conti took the name Innocent in part to honor that lineage.

faqs.question: How did Innocent XIII treat the Jesuits?
faqs.answer: He pressed the Jesuits firmly to obey papal rulings against the Chinese Rites and, according to standard accounts, threatened to stop the order from admitting new members. His death in 1724 left the matter unresolved.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict XIII was Pietro Francesco Orsini, a Dominican friar from a great Roman noble family, who reigned from 29 May 1724 to 21 February 1730. A devout pastor who had been archbishop of Benevento for nearly four decades, he is now a Servant of God, though his reign was marred by his trust in the corrupt Cardinal Niccolò Coscia.

sections.h2: An Orsini Heir Who Became a Dominican Friar
paras: Pietro Francesco Orsini was born in 1649 at Gravina in Apulia, the eldest son of the Duke of Gravina. As a young man he renounced his inheritance to join the Order of Preachers, taking the religious name Vincenzo, despite strong family opposition. His relative Clement X made him a cardinal in 1672, when he was only in his early twenties.

He was the third and last member of the Orsini family to become pope. On his election he first planned to be called Benedict XIV, but changed the number to XIII to make clear that Pedro de Luna, who had used the name Benedict XIII during the Western Schism, was not a legitimate pope.

sections.h2: Thirty-Eight Years as Archbishop of Benevento
paras: Before his election Orsini served as archbishop of Benevento from 1686, a see he continued to hold even as pope. He became known as a tireless pastor: he held diocesan synods, visited parishes, rebuilt churches, and helped the city recover after a destructive earthquake in 1688, which he survived when part of the archbishop's residence collapsed.

As pope he tried to bring the same pastoral manner to Rome. He lived simply, often preferred the plain habit of his order, visited the sick, and celebrated liturgies personally. In 1725 he held a Roman council aimed at the reform of clerical life, and he presided over the Jubilee of 1725, the year the Spanish Steps were opened.

sections.h2: The Coscia Scandal
paras: Benedict XIII had little experience of temporal government and entrusted much of it to Niccolò Coscia, a former secretary from Benevento whom he made a cardinal. Coscia and his associates used their positions for personal gain, damaging the finances of the Papal States and the reputation of the reign.

The pope appears not to have recognized the abuses. After his death, Coscia was tried under Clement XII, stripped of his offices, fined, and imprisoned. Historians generally contrast the personal holiness of Benedict XIII with the poor administration carried out in his name.

sections.h2: Saints Raised to the Altars and an Open Cause
paras: Benedict XIII canonized several saints whose cults remain widespread, including the young Jesuits Aloysius Gonzaga and Stanislaus Kostka and the Carmelite mystic John of the Cross. He also extended certain feasts, and in 1725 he lifted the penalties that had forbidden the use of tobacco in St. Peter's Basilica.
He died in February 1730 and was buried in the Dominican basilica of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome. A cause for his beatification has been opened, which is why he bears the title Servant of God.

keyFacts: Born Pietro Francesco Orsini at Gravina in Puglia in 1649
Reigned 29 May 1724 – 21 February 1730
Dominican friar with the religious name Vincenzo
Archbishop of Benevento from 1686, keeping the see as pope
Canonized Aloysius Gonzaga, Stanislaus Kostka and John of the Cross
Buried in Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome; title Servant of God

faqs.question: Why is he Benedict XIII and not Benedict XIV?
faqs.answer: The name Benedict XIII had been used by Pedro de Luna, an antipope of the Western Schism. Orsini took the number XIII himself, signaling that the Church did not count Luna as a true pope.

faqs.question: Who was Cardinal Coscia?
faqs.answer: Niccolò Coscia was Benedict XIII's trusted aide from Benevento, made a cardinal, who abused his power for financial gain. After the pope's death he was tried, deprived of his offices and imprisoned.

faqs.question: Is Benedict XIII on the path to sainthood?
faqs.answer: Yes. His beatification cause has been opened, giving him the title Servant of God, in recognition of his reputation for personal holiness and pastoral zeal.

directAnswer: Pope Clement XII was Lorenzo Corsini of Florence, elected at 78, who reigned from 12 July 1730 to 6 February 1740 despite becoming blind. He commissioned the Trevi Fountain and the façade of St. John Lateran, opened the Capitoline Museums to the public, and in 1738 issued In eminenti, the first papal condemnation of Freemasonry.

sections.h2: A Florentine Banker's Son in Papal Service
paras: Lorenzo Corsini was born in Florence in 1652 into a wealthy, distinguished family. After studying law, he purchased a Curial office, as was customary, and rose through the papal administration, including a term as treasurer of the Apostolic Camera. Clement XI made him a cardinal in 1706.

By the 1730 conclave Corsini was elderly and in poor health. Within a few years of his election he lost his sight almost completely and was often confined to bed, yet he continued to receive officials and direct business with the help of his nephew, Cardinal Neri Corsini.

sections.h2: Repairing the Finances and Judging Coscia
paras: Clement XII inherited the damage done under his predecessor by Cardinal Niccolò Coscia. He had Coscia prosecuted, and the cardinal was condemned to prison and made to restore funds. The pope also tried to restore the treasury, among other measures reintroducing the public lottery, which raised funds that were applied to building projects and charity.

Politically his reign was difficult. The Papal States were powerless during the War of the Polish Succession, foreign armies crossed papal territory, and Rome lost its feudal claims over Parma and Piacenza.

sections.h2: The Trevi Fountain, the Lateran and the Capitoline
paras: Clement XII left a deep mark on the face of Rome. In 1732 he held a competition for a new fountain at the end of the Aqua Virgo aqueduct, which Nicola Salvi won; work on the Trevi Fountain began that year and was finished only in 1762. He also commissioned Alessandro Galilei's monumental façade for the Archbasilica of St. John Lateran, the pope's cathedral, completed in 1735, and built the Corsini Chapel inside it, where he is buried.

In 1734 he opened the Capitoline Museums to the public, a step often cited as the beginning of the public museum in Europe. He also added to the Vatican Library's collections of manuscripts and antiquities.

sections.h2: In eminenti and the Condemnation of Freemasonry
paras: On 28 April 1738 Clement XII issued In eminenti apostolatus specula, forbidding Catholics to join Masonic lodges under pain of excommunication. The pope cited the secrecy and oaths of the lodges and their gathering of men of differing religions in a way that, he judged, endangered the faith. It was the first of many papal condemnations of Freemasonry, renewed by later popes into the twentieth century.

He also canonized Vincent de Paul in 1737 and worked to reconcile Eastern Christians, including Maronite and Coptic communities, with Rome. He died in February 1740, after nearly a decade on the throne.

Condemned Freemasonry in In eminenti apostolatus specula (1738)

faqs.question: Did Clement XII build the Trevi Fountain?
faqs.answer: He commissioned it. Clement XII chose Nicola Salvi's design in a 1732 competition and work began that year, but the fountain was not completed until 1762 under Clement XIII.

faqs.question: Why did Clement XII condemn Freemasonry?
faqs.answer: In In eminenti (1738) he cited the lodges' secrecy, binding oaths and indifference to religious differences as dangers to faith, and forbade Catholics to join them under penalty of excommunication.

faqs.question: Was Clement XII blind?
faqs.answer: Yes. He lost his sight early in his pontificate and was often bedridden, governing with the help of his nephew, Cardinal Neri Corsini.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict XIV was Prospero Lambertini of Bologna, one of the most learned canon lawyers ever to become pope, who reigned from 17 August 1740 to 3 May 1758. He wrote the standard work on beatification and canonization, settled the Chinese and Malabar rites controversies, reformed seminaries and church discipline, and won admiration even from Enlightenment critics of the Church.

sections.h2: Prospero Lambertini, Canonist and Promoter of the Faith
paras: Prospero Lambertini was born in Bologna in 1675 and earned doctorates in theology and law while still young. In Rome he served for many years as Promoter of the Faith, the official charged with examining the arguments for causes of beatification and canonization.

That experience produced his great treatise on the beatification and canonization of the servants of God, which set out the evidentiary standards for miracles and heroic virtue. It remained the essential reference for saint-making procedures long after his death. He was made a cardinal in 1728, became archbishop of Bologna in 1731, and was known there as a conscientious pastor with a lively wit.

sections.h2: Elected After a Six-Month Conclave
paras: The conclave of 1740 dragged on for about six months as factions failed to agree. Lambertini, who had joked about the deadlock, was finally chosen as a compromise and took the name Benedict in honor of Benedict XIII, who had made him a cardinal.

He set a conciliatory tone with the Catholic monarchs, concluding concordats with Sardinia, Naples and Spain. The Spanish concordat of 1753 conceded broad royal rights of patronage, a pragmatic choice that preserved peace at the cost of papal control over appointments.

sections.h2: Ending the Rites Controversies and Teaching on Usury
paras: Benedict XIV closed the long debate on missionary adaptation. In Ex quo singulari (1742) he confirmed the prohibition of the Chinese Rites and required missionaries to take an oath to observe it, and in Omnium sollicitudinum (1744) he ruled similarly on the Malabar Rites in India. In Allatae sunt (1755) he insisted, on the other hand, that the legitimate rites of the Eastern Catholic Churches be respected and not latinized.

His encyclical Vix pervenit (1745), addressed to the bishops of Italy, restated Church teaching that taking interest simply by reason of a loan is usury, while recognizing that other legitimate titles could justify a return. Early in his reign he issued Ubi primum (1740) on the duties of bishops, often cited as one of the first documents in the modern encyclical form.

sections.h2: Scholarship, Science and Liturgical Reform
paras: Benedict XIV was a patron of learning. He founded academies in Rome for the study of Roman antiquities and history, supported the University of Bologna and its scientific institute, and expanded the collections of the Vatican Library and museums. He also reformed seminary education and worked on a revision of the Roman Breviary and the calendar of feasts, though the breviary reform was not completed.

The 1758 edition of the Index of Forbidden Books, prepared during his reign, dropped the general prohibition of books teaching the motion of the earth, although specific bans on certain works remained. Voltaire dedicated his play Mahomet to Benedict XIV, and the pope's courteous reply became famous. He died in May 1758, widely regarded as one of the ablest popes of the century.

Reigned 17 August 1740 – 3 May 1758
Author of the classic treatise on beatification and canonization
Confirmed the ban on the Chinese Rites in Ex quo singulari (1742)
Issued Vix pervenit (1745) on usury
Concluded concordats with Sardinia, Naples and Spain

faqs.question: Why is Benedict XIV important for the canonization of saints?
faqs.answer: As Promoter of the Faith and later as a scholar, he wrote the authoritative treatise on beatification and canonization, setting out standards for evaluating heroic virtue and miracles that guided the Church for centuries.

faqs.question: What did Benedict XIV teach in Vix pervenit?
faqs.answer: Vix pervenit (1745) taught that charging interest merely because money is lent is usury, while acknowledging that separate legitimate titles, such as other contracts or losses, could justify a gain.

faqs.question: How did Benedict XIV treat the Eastern Catholic Churches?
faqs.answer: In Allatae sunt (1755) he directed that the traditional rites of Eastern Catholics be respected and preserved, and that missionaries not pressure them to adopt Latin customs.

directAnswer: Pope Clement XIII was Carlo della Torre di Rezzonico, a Venetian and former bishop of Padua, who reigned from 6 July 1758 to 2 February 1769. His pontificate was dominated by the campaign of the Catholic Bourbon courts and Portugal against the Society of Jesus, which he defended in the 1765 bull Apostolicum pascendi.

sections.h2: A Pastoral Bishop from Venice
paras: Carlo della Torre di Rezzonico was born in Venice in 1693 to a wealthy family that had recently purchased admission to the Venetian nobility. He studied with the Jesuits in Bologna, took a law degree at Padua, and served in the Curia before Clement XII made him a cardinal in 1737.

From 1743 he was bishop of Padua, where he gained a reputation for personal piety, generosity to the poor, and careful attention to his clergy. These qualities, more than political skill, recommended him to the cardinals in 1758.

sections.h2: The Storm Against the Jesuits
paras: Clement XIII's reign coincided with a coordinated assault on the Society of Jesus. Portugal, under the minister Pombal, expelled the Jesuits in 1759. In France the Parlement of Paris moved against them and the crown dissolved the order in the kingdom in 1764. Spain expelled the Jesuits in 1767, followed by Naples and Parma, and many exiled Jesuits were shipped to the Papal States.

The pope refused to abandon the order. In January 1765 he issued Apostolicum pascendi, solemnly reaffirming the Society's approval and praising its work in education and the missions. The bull was rejected or suppressed by several governments, and it did not halt the campaign.

sections.h2: The Parma Crisis and the Seizure of Avignon
paras: In 1768 Clement XIII condemned anticlerical decrees issued by the Duchy of Parma, a small state ruled by a Bourbon prince. The Bourbon courts treated this as an affront to the whole family. France occupied the papal enclave of Avignon and the Venaissin, and Naples seized Benevento and Pontecorvo.
The ambassadors of the Bourbon powers then formally demanded the complete suppression of the Jesuits. Clement XIII died in February 1769 before giving an answer, leaving the crisis to his successor.

sections.h2: Devotion to the Sacred Heart and Canova's Monument
paras: Amid these conflicts Clement XIII encouraged popular devotion. In 1765 he approved a feast and liturgy of the Sacred Heart of Jesus for petitioners in Poland and for a Roman archconfraternity, an important early step toward the universal feast later established by Pius IX.

He also issued encyclicals warning against irreligious books of the Enlightenment. His tomb in St. Peter's Basilica, carved by Antonio Canova and completed in 1792, is regarded as one of the masterpieces of Neoclassical sculpture.

keyFacts: Born Carlo della Torre di Rezzonico in Venice in 1693
Reigned 6 July 1758 – 2 February 1769
Bishop of Padua from 1743
Defended the Jesuits in Apostolicum pascendi (1765)
Approved a feast of the Sacred Heart for Poland and a Roman confraternity in 1765
Tomb in St. Peter's carved by Antonio Canova

faqs.question: How did Clement XIII respond to the expulsion of the Jesuits?
faqs.answer: He defended them. As Portugal, France, Spain and other states expelled the order, Clement XIII issued Apostolicum pascendi in 1765, reaffirming papal approval of the Society of Jesus.

faqs.question: Why did France seize Avignon during his reign?
faqs.answer: After Clement XIII condemned anticlerical laws of the Bourbon-ruled Duchy of Parma in 1768, France occupied the papal territory of Avignon and Naples seized Benevento, as pressure on the pope to suppress the Jesuits.

faqs.question: What was Clement XIII's connection to the Sacred Heart?
faqs.answer: In 1765 he granted permission for a Mass and feast of the Sacred Heart in Poland and for a Roman archconfraternity, among the first official liturgical approvals of the devotion.

directAnswer: Pope Clement XIV was Lorenzo Ganganelli, a Conventual Franciscan friar who reigned from 19 May 1769 to 22 September 1774. Under heavy pressure from the Catholic Bourbon monarchies, he suppressed the Society of Jesus in 1773 with the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, and he founded what became the Pio-Clementine Museum at the Vatican.

sections.h2: Friar Lorenzo Ganganelli
paras: Giovanni Vincenzo Antonio Ganganelli was born in 1705 at Santarcangelo di Romagna, the son of a country doctor. He entered the Conventual Franciscans as a teenager, taking the name Lorenzo, and became a respected theologian and teacher, serving later as a consultor of the Holy Office.
Clement XIII made him a cardinal in 1759. He was the only friar of his order in the College of Cardinals and was regarded as learned, mild and politically cautious.

sections.h2: A Conclave Shaped by the Jesuit Question
paras: The conclave of 1769 met under strong pressure from France, Spain, Naples and Portugal, whose ambassadors wanted a pope willing to suppress the Jesuits. It lasted more than three months. Ganganelli was elected, and historians have long debated whether he gave any assurances beforehand; no reliable evidence shows a formal promise, though the courts clearly expected him to act.

Once pope, Clement XIV sought to repair relations with the Catholic powers. He stopped the annual public reading of the bull In Coena Domini, which had long irritated rulers, and restored diplomatic contact with Portugal.

sections.h2: Dominus ac Redemptor and the Suppression of 1773
paras: For four years Clement delayed, while the Bourbon courts, led by Spain, pressed him and kept possession of Avignon and Benevento. On 21 July 1773 he signed the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, which dissolved the Society of Jesus throughout the world. The document did not condemn Jesuit doctrine or the morals of its members; it presented the suppression as necessary for the peace of the Church.

The Jesuit superior general, Lorenzo Ricci, was imprisoned in Castel Sant'Angelo, where he died in 1775. In Prussia and Russia, whose non-Catholic rulers refused to promulgate the brief, small groups of Jesuits continued to exist, which later made possible the order's restoration by Pius VII in 1814. After the suppression, France and Naples returned Avignon and Benevento to the Holy See.

sections.h2: The Pio-Clementine Museum and a Troubled End
paras: Clement XIV took a strong interest in classical antiquities and began the reorganization of the Vatican's collections of sculpture into a new museum. His successor Pius VI greatly expanded it, and it is still called the Pio-Clementine Museum after both popes.

Clement's health declined in 1774, and he died in September of that year. Rumors of poisoning circulated, but the autopsy and later historians have not supported them. He is buried in the Basilica of the Twelve Holy Apostles in Rome, the church of his Franciscan order, in a tomb by Antonio Canova.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Vincenzo Antonio Ganganelli at Santarcangelo di Romagna in 1705
Reigned 19 May 1769 – 22 September 1774
Conventual Franciscan with the religious name Lorenzo
Suppressed the Society of Jesus with Dominus ac Redemptor (21 July 1773)
Began the Vatican's Pio-Clementine Museum
Buried in the Basilica of the Holy Apostles, Rome, in a tomb by Canova

faqs.question: Why did Clement XIV suppress the Jesuits?
faqs.answer: He acted after years of pressure from the Catholic monarchies of Spain, France, Portugal and Naples, which had already expelled the order. Dominus ac Redemptor justified the suppression as necessary for peace in the Church rather than as a condemnation of Jesuit teaching.

faqs.question: Did the Jesuits disappear completely after 1773?
faqs.answer: No. In Russia and Prussia the rulers did not promulgate the brief, so Jesuit communities survived there. This continuity allowed Pius VII to restore the Society worldwide in 1814.

faqs.question: Was Clement XIV poisoned?
faqs.answer: Rumors of poisoning spread after his death in 1774, but they were not borne out by the medical examination at the time and are generally rejected by historians.

directAnswer: Pope Pius VI was Giovanni Angelo Braschi of Cesena, who reigned from 15 February 1775 to 29 August 1799, one of the longest pontificates up to that time. He erected the first Catholic diocese in the United States at Baltimore, condemned the French Revolution's Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and died a prisoner of the French Republic at Valence.

sections.h2: Treasurer of the Apostolic Camera to Pope
paras: Giovanni Angelo Braschi was born in Cesena in the Romagna in 1717 to a family of minor nobility. He studied law, entered papal service as secretary to Cardinal Ruffo and later to Benedict XIV, and served as treasurer of the Apostolic Camera, the papal finance office. Clement XIV made him a cardinal in 1773.

He was elected in February 1775 after a conclave of more than four months, still dominated by the aftermath of the Jesuit suppression. Handsome, cultivated and fond of ceremony, he opened the Jubilee of 1775 soon after his election.

sections.h2: Builder and Patron in Papal Rome
paras: Pius VI was the last pope to sponsor art and building on the scale of the Renaissance and Baroque papacy. He greatly expanded the Vatican museum of classical sculpture begun by Clement XIV, which bears both their names as the Pio-Clementine Museum, built the new sacristy of St. Peter's Basilica, and erected ancient obelisks in Roman squares.

He also undertook an ambitious drainage of the Pontine Marshes south of Rome, which achieved partial success. Critics noted his generosity to his nephew Luigi Braschi Onesti, for whom the Palazzo Braschi in Rome was built.

sections.h2: Josephinism, Pistoia and the First American Bishop
paras: The Habsburg Emperor Joseph II sought to control the Church in his lands, closing monasteries and regulating seminaries and worship. In 1782 Pius VI made the unusual journey to Vienna to plead with the emperor in person. He was received with honor but obtained few concessions.

In 1794 he issued the bull Auctorem fidei, condemning propositions of the Synod of Pistoia in Tuscany, which had adopted Jansenist and state-church positions. For American Catholics his reign has particular significance: in 1789 he erected the Diocese of Baltimore, the first in the United States, and confirmed John Carroll as its first bishop.

sections.h2: The French Revolution and Death in Exile
paras: When revolutionary France imposed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which subjected the Church to the state and required clergy to swear an oath to it, Pius VI condemned it in 1791. The breach led to the persecution of loyal clergy in France, and relations with the Republic collapsed.

In 1796 French armies under Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Italy, and the 1797 Treaty of Tolentino forced the pope to cede territory and pay heavy indemnities. In February 1798 French troops occupied Rome and proclaimed a republic. The aged and ailing pope was removed from the city, held in Tuscany, and then carried across the Alps to Valence in France, where he died on 29 August 1799. His remains were later returned to Rome and rest in St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Angelo Braschi in Cesena in 1717
Reigned 15 February 1775 – 29 August 1799
Erected the Diocese of Baltimore and confirmed John Carroll as bishop (1789)
Condemned the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1791)
Condemned the Synod of Pistoia in Auctorem fidei (1794)
Died a prisoner of the French at Valence, France

faqs.question: What did Pius VI do for the Church in the United States?
faqs.answer: In 1789 he established the Diocese of Baltimore, the first Catholic diocese in the United States, and confirmed Father John Carroll, chosen by the American clergy, as its first bishop.

faqs.question: Why did Pius VI die in France?
faqs.answer: French revolutionary forces occupied Rome in 1798 and removed the pope. After being held in Tuscany he was taken to Valence in France, where he died in August 1799 at the age of 81.

faqs.question: Why did Pius VI travel to Vienna?
faqs.answer: In 1782 he went to Vienna to persuade Emperor Joseph II to moderate reforms that placed the Church under state control. The visit was cordial but changed little.

directAnswer: Pope Pius VII was Barnaba Chiaramonti, a Benedictine monk elected in Venice who reigned from 14 March 1800 to 20 August 1823. He negotiated the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon, attended his imperial coronation, endured five years of captivity under French control, restored the Jesuits in 1814, and is now a Servant of God.

sections.h2: Dom Gregorio, Benedictine of Cesena
paras: Barnaba Niccolò Maria Luigi Chiaramonti was born in Cesena in 1742 into a noble family. At sixteen he entered the Benedictine abbey of Santa Maria del Monte, taking the name Gregorio, and became a teacher of theology. His fellow townsman Pius VI named him bishop of Tivoli and then of Imola, and created him a cardinal in 1785.

As bishop of Imola during the French occupation of northern Italy, he preached a Christmas homily in 1797 arguing that the democratic form of government was not in itself opposed to the Gospel. The remark later helped make him acceptable to several parties.

sections.h2: A Conclave in Venice and the Concordat of 1801
paras: With Rome occupied after the death of Pius VI, the cardinals met under Austrian protection in the Benedictine monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice. After more than three months they elected Chiaramonti in March 1800. He soon returned to Rome and appointed Ercole Consalvi as his secretary of state, a partnership that defined the reign.

Pius VII and Consalvi negotiated the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon Bonaparte, then First Consul. It restored public Catholic worship in France and reorganized its dioceses, though Napoleon's unilateral Organic Articles soon added restrictions the pope never accepted. In December 1804 Pius traveled to Paris for Napoleon's coronation as emperor; Napoleon crowned himself after the pope's anointing.

sections.h2: Captivity at Savona and Fontainebleau
paras: Relations broke down when Pius refused to join Napoleon's continental blockade against Britain. French troops occupied Rome in 1808, and in 1809 Napoleon annexed the Papal States. When the pope excommunicated those responsible, he was arrested in the Quirinal Palace in July 1809 and taken into captivity, first at Savona on the Italian Riviera.

In 1812 he was moved to Fontainebleau near Paris. Isolated and ill, he signed a draft agreement in 1813 but soon retracted it. Only after Napoleon's defeats was the pope released, and he reentered Rome in May 1814 to great acclaim. Later he gave shelter in Rome to members of Napoleon's family after the emperor's fall.

sections.h2: Restoring the Jesuits and Rebuilding the Church
paras: On 7 August 1814 Pius VII issued the bull Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum, restoring the Society of Jesus throughout the world. At the Congress of Vienna Consalvi recovered most of the Papal States, and the pope reorganized their administration, including creating the Papal Carabinieri in 1816. He concluded concordats with several states and supported the rebuilding of dioceses and religious life.

The Church in the United States also grew under him: in 1808 he raised Baltimore to an archdiocese and created the dioceses of New York, Boston, Philadelphia and Bardstown. He died in August 1823 after a fall, and his cause for beatification has been opened, giving him the title Servant of God.

keyFacts: Born Barnaba Chiaramonti in Cesena in 1742; Benedictine name Gregorio
Reigned 14 March 1800 – 20 August 1823; elected in Venice
Concluded the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon
Held captive at Savona and Fontainebleau, 1809–1814
Restored the Jesuits in Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum (1814)
Made Baltimore an archdiocese and created four U.S. dioceses in 1808

faqs.question: Did Pius VII crown Napoleon?
faqs.answer: No. Pius VII attended the 1804 coronation in Notre-Dame and anointed Napoleon, but Napoleon placed the crown on his own head and then crowned Josephine.

faqs.question: Why was Pius VII imprisoned?
faqs.answer: After Napoleon annexed the Papal States in 1809 and the pope excommunicated those responsible, French forces arrested him. He was held at Savona and later Fontainebleau until 1814.

faqs.question: How did Pius VII shape the Church in America?
faqs.answer: In 1808 he made Baltimore the first U.S. archdiocese and created the dioceses of New York, Boston, Philadelphia and Bardstown, Kentucky.

directAnswer: Pope Leo XII was Annibale della Genga, a former papal diplomat from the Marche who reigned from 28 September 1823 to 10 February 1829. Strict and reform-minded, he celebrated the Jubilee of 1825, placed education in the Papal States under close Church supervision with a leading role for the Jesuits, and condemned secret societies and Bible societies.

sections.h2: Annibale della Genga, Nuncio in Germany
paras: Annibale Sermattei della Genga was born in 1760 at the family castle of Genga, near Fabriano in the Marche, then part of the Papal States. After studies in Rome he was ordained and entered papal service, becoming a private secretary to Pius VI.

Much of his career was spent in diplomacy in German-speaking lands, as nuncio in Lucerne, Cologne and Munich, and he was sent on missions connected with the Napoleonic settlement. Pius VII made him a cardinal in 1816 and vicar general of Rome in 1820.

sections.h2: The Zelanti Conclave of 1823
paras: Della Genga was the candidate of the zelanti, the cardinals who favored a stricter, more religious policy than that of Cardinal Consalvi. Elected in September 1823 in frail health, he replaced Consalvi as secretary of state, although the two were reported to have reconciled before Consalvi's death in 1824.

In the Papal States Leo XII reversed many reforms of the Napoleonic era. He restricted the Jewish community of Rome to the ghetto again, enforced strict public morality, and dealt harshly with members of the Carbonari and other secret revolutionary societies. These measures made him unpopular with many Romans.

sections.h2: Quod divina sapientia and the Jubilee of 1825
paras: In the 1824 bull Quod divina sapientia Leo XII reorganized schools and universities throughout the Papal States under a congregation of studies, placing education under close ecclesiastical supervision. He returned the Roman College to the Jesuits, restored only a decade earlier, and assigned them a central role in teaching.

Leo XII proclaimed the Holy Year of 1825, the first jubilee celebrated since 1775 because of the revolutionary upheavals. Despite the hesitation of some governments, pilgrims came to Rome in large numbers, and the pope personally took part in its devotions. He also pressed forward the rebuilding of the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls after the fire of 1823.

sections.h2: Condemning Secret Societies and Bible Societies
paras: In his first encyclical, Ubi primum (1824), Leo XII warned against religious indifferentism and the Bible societies that were distributing vernacular Scripture without Church-approved notes. In 1826 the apostolic constitution Quo graviora renewed earlier papal condemnations of Freemasonry and other secret societies.

Leo XII also took steps to provide bishops for the newly independent states of Latin America, a delicate question given Spain's claims of patronage. He died in February 1829 and is buried in St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Annibale della Genga at Genga, near Fabriano, in 1760
Reigned 28 September 1823 – 10 February 1829
Former nuncio in Lucerne, Cologne and Munich
Reorganized education in the Papal States in Quod divina sapientia (1824)
Celebrated the Holy Year of 1825
Condemned Freemasonry in Quo graviora (1826)

faqs.question: Why was the Jubilee of 1825 significant?
faqs.answer: It was the first Holy Year held in fifty years, since war and revolution had prevented the jubilee of 1800. Leo XII insisted on holding it as a sign of the Church's recovery.

faqs.question: What was Leo XII's policy in the Papal States?
faqs.answer: He governed strictly, undoing many Napoleonic-era reforms, tightening public morality, reimposing restrictions on Rome's Jews, and suppressing revolutionary secret societies.

faqs.question: What did Leo XII teach about Bible societies?
faqs.answer: In Ubi primum (1824) he warned against societies distributing vernacular Bibles without approved notes, which he believed encouraged private interpretation detached from Church teaching.

directAnswer: Pope Pius VIII was Francesco Saverio Castiglioni, a canon lawyer from Cingoli who reigned only from 31 March 1829 to 30 November 1830. In his brief pontificate he condemned indifferentism and secret societies in the encyclical Traditi humilitati, welcomed Catholic Emancipation in Britain, and recognized Louis Philippe as king of the French after the July Revolution.

sections.h2: Canonist, Bishop and Prisoner of Napoleon
paras: Francesco Saverio Castiglioni was born in 1761 at Cingoli in the Marche to a noble family. He studied canon law and became a respected specialist. As bishop of Montalto he refused the oath of allegiance demanded by Napoleon's regime and was imprisoned in France for several years.

After the restoration Pius VII made him a cardinal in 1816 and named him bishop of Cesena and later of Frascati. Pius VII is said to have regarded him as a fitting successor, and he was already a serious candidate in the conclave of 1823.

sections.h2: Traditi humilitati and Mixed Marriages
paras: In his only encyclical, Traditi humilitati (1829), Pius VIII warned against religious indifferentism, the view that all religions are equally valid, and against secret societies and the distribution of unapproved vernacular Bible translations. He also urged care in the education of youth and the formation of clergy.

In 1830 he issued a brief addressed to bishops in Prussia's Rhineland provinces on mixed marriages between Catholics and Protestants. It allowed priests to be present at such marriages without the usual blessing when Catholic upbringing of the children could not be guaranteed. The question later grew into a serious conflict between the Church and the Prussian state.

sections.h2: Catholic Emancipation and the July Revolution
paras: In April 1829, weeks after his election, the British Parliament passed the Catholic Relief Act, which allowed Catholics in Great Britain and Ireland to sit in Parliament and hold most public offices. Pius VIII welcomed the measure, which owed much to the campaign of Daniel O'Connell in Ireland.

In July 1830 revolution in Paris overthrew King Charles X. Despite the anticlerical tone of the uprising, Pius VIII recognized Louis Philippe as king of the French, a pragmatic decision meant to protect the Church in France. In poor health throughout his reign, he died in November 1830 after twenty months as pope.

keyFacts: Born Francesco Saverio Castiglioni at Cingoli in 1761
Reigned 31 March 1829 – 30 November 1830
Imprisoned under Napoleon for refusing an oath of allegiance
Issued the encyclical Traditi humilitati (1829)
Reign saw Catholic Emancipation in Britain (1829)
Recognized Louis Philippe as king of the French (1830)

faqs.question: What did Pius VIII's encyclical Traditi humilitati address?
faqs.answer: It warned against religious indifferentism, secret societies, and unapproved Bible translations, and called for sound education and clerical formation. It was the only encyclical of his short reign.

faqs.question: How did Pius VIII respond to Catholic Emancipation?
faqs.answer: He welcomed the British Catholic Relief Act of 1829, which allowed Catholics in Britain and Ireland to sit in Parliament and hold most public offices.

faqs.question: Why did Pius VIII recognize Louis Philippe?
faqs.answer: After the 1830 July Revolution in France, he judged that recognizing the new king would best protect French Catholics, despite the revolution's anticlerical character.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory XVI was Bartolomeo Alberto Cappellari, a Camaldolese monk who reigned from 2 February 1831 to 1 June 1846 and was the last pope elected who was not yet a bishop. He condemned liberal ideas in Mirari vos, denounced the slave trade in In supremo apostolatus, strongly supported the missions, and resisted political reform in the Papal States.

sections.h2: Dom Mauro, Camaldolese Monk
paras: Bartolomeo Alberto Cappellari was born in 1765 at Belluno, then in the Republic of Venice. He entered the Camaldolese Benedictines at San Michele di Murano in Venice, taking the name Mauro, and became a theologian. In 1799 he published a book defending papal authority and infallibility, The Triumph of the Holy See.

He later became abbot of San Gregorio al Celio in Rome and in 1826 was made a cardinal and prefect of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith. He was elected in February 1831 after a fifty-day conclave and, being only a priest, was consecrated a bishop after his election, the last pope of whom this is true.

sections.h2: Revolt in the Papal States
paras: Within days of his election revolution broke out in Bologna and other cities of the Papal States. Gregory XVI relied on Austrian troops to restore order, and French forces occupied Ancona in response. The European powers urged administrative reforms, but the pope and his secretaries of state allowed only limited changes.

His government remained conservative and was widely criticized for its police measures and resistance to lay participation. Gregory's distrust of modern innovations is well documented, though some anecdotes about it are of doubtful origin.

sections.h2: Mirari vos and the Lamennais Affair
paras: In the encyclical Mirari vos (1832) Gregory XVI condemned religious indifferentism and rejected unlimited freedom of conscience and of the press, as well as calls for the separation of Church and state. The letter was directed in part at the French priest Félicité de Lamennais and his journal L'Avenir, which urged the Church to embrace liberty and democracy.

When Lamennais broke with Rome, Gregory condemned his book Words of a Believer in the encyclical Singulari nos (1834). The episode set the pattern for tensions between the papacy and Catholic liberalism for the rest of the century.

sections.h2: The Slave Trade, the Missions and the Vatican Museums
paras: In the apostolic letter In supremo apostolatus (1839) Gregory XVI condemned the trade in African and Indigenous slaves and forbade Catholics to defend or engage in it. Drawing on his years at Propaganda Fide, he gave strong support to the missions, creating many new dioceses and apostolic vicariates in Asia, Africa and the Americas, including a number in the United States, and encouraging the formation of native clergy.

He also founded the Gregorian Etruscan Museum and the Gregorian Egyptian Museum in the Vatican, which still bear his name. During his reign, in 1835, the remaining works of Galileo and Copernicus were left off the Index of Forbidden Books. He died in June 1846 and is buried in St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Bartolomeo Alberto Cappellari at Belluno in 1765; Camaldolese name Mauro
Reigned 2 February 1831 – 1 June 1846
Last pope elected while not yet a bishop
Issued Mirari vos (1832) and Singulari nos (1834)
Condemned the slave trade in In supremo apostolatus (1839)
Founded the Vatican's Etruscan and Egyptian museums

faqs.question: What did Gregory XVI teach about slavery?
faqs.answer: In In supremo apostolatus (1839) he condemned the slave trade and forbade Catholics to take part in or defend trafficking in Black Africans or Indigenous peoples.

faqs.question: Why is Gregory XVI notable as the last non-bishop elected pope?
faqs.answer: He was a priest and monk, not a bishop, when elected in 1831, and received episcopal consecration afterward. Every pope since has already been a bishop at election.

faqs.question: What was Mirari vos?
faqs.answer: Mirari vos (1832) was Gregory XVI's encyclical condemning religious indifferentism and unrestricted freedoms of conscience and the press, aimed largely at the Catholic liberalism of Félicité de Lamennais.

directAnswer: Blessed Pius IX was Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, who reigned from 16 June 1846 to 7 February 1878, the longest verified pontificate in Church history. He defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, convened the First Vatican Council, which defined papal infallibility, and lost the Papal States to the Kingdom of Italy. He was beatified in 2000.

sections.h2: From Senigallia to the Chair of Peter
paras: Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti was born in Senigallia in 1792 to a family of minor nobility. Epilepsy in his youth nearly prevented his ordination, but he was ordained in 1819. He served on a papal mission to Chile in the 1820s, an experience that made him the first future pope to visit the Americas, and later became archbishop of Spoleto and bishop of Imola. Gregory XVI made him a cardinal in 1840.

Elected in June 1846 at 54, he was initially greeted as a liberal reformer after granting an amnesty to political prisoners. The revolutions of 1848 changed that. After the assassination of his minister Pellegrino Rossi, Pius fled Rome to Gaeta in the Kingdom of Naples and returned in 1850 only with French military support, convinced that liberal nationalism threatened the Church.

sections.h2: Ineffabilis Deus and the Immaculate Conception
paras: After consulting the bishops of the world, Pius IX solemnly defined on 8 December 1854, in the bull Ineffabilis Deus, that the Blessed Virgin Mary was preserved free from all stain of original sin from the first moment of her conception. In 1858 the apparitions at Lourdes, in which the Lady identified herself as the Immaculate Conception, were received by many Catholics as heavenly confirmation.

American Catholics have a special bond with this teaching: the U.S. bishops had chosen Mary under the title of the Immaculate Conception as patroness of the nation in 1846, a choice Pius IX approved the following year.

sections.h2: The Syllabus of Errors and the First Vatican Council
paras: In 1864 Pius IX issued the encyclical Quanta cura with an attached Syllabus of Errors, a list of eighty propositions drawn from earlier documents that he condemned, including rationalism, indifferentism and the claim that the pope should reconcile himself with liberalism and modern civilization. Its sweeping wording caused controversy, and many bishops explained it in more nuanced terms.

On 8 December 1869 he opened the First Vatican Council, the first ecumenical council since Trent. In the constitution Dei Filius it taught on faith and reason, and on 18 July 1870 the constitution Pastor aeternus defined papal primacy and the infallibility of the pope when he solemnly defines a doctrine of faith or morals ex cathedra. The council was suspended when war broke out and Italian troops approached Rome.

sections.h2: The Loss of Rome and the Prisoner of the Vatican
paras: On 20 September 1870 Italian forces entered Rome, ending more than a thousand years of papal temporal rule. Pius IX refused to accept the loss or the Italian government's Law of Guarantees and withdrew within the Vatican, calling himself a prisoner. His successors maintained that position until the Lateran Treaty of 1929.

His reign also saw controversy, notably the Mortara case of 1858, in which a Jewish boy secretly baptized by a servant was removed from his family by papal authorities, an act widely condemned then and since.

sections.h2: Devotion, Missions and Beatification
paras: Pius IX extended the feast of the Sacred Heart to the universal Church in 1856 and in 1870 proclaimed St. Joseph patron of the Universal Church. He restored the Catholic hierarchy in England in 1850 and the Netherlands in 1853, and in 1859 he opened the Pontifical North American College in Rome to train priests for the United States.

He was the first pope to be photographed. He died in February 1878 after more than 31 years as pope. Pope John Paul II beatified him on 3 September 2000, together with John XXIII, and his liturgical memorial is kept on February 7.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti in Senigallia in 1792
Reigned 16 June 1846 – 7 February 1878, the longest verified pontificate
Defined the Immaculate Conception in Ineffabilis Deus (8 December 1854)
Issued Quanta cura and the Syllabus of Errors (1864)
Convened the First Vatican Council, which defined papal infallibility (1870)
Beatified by John Paul II on 3 September 2000

faqs.question: What did the First Vatican Council define under Pius IX?
faqs.answer: In Pastor aeternus (1870) it defined the primacy of the pope and his infallibility when he speaks ex cathedra, solemnly defining a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church. It also taught on faith and reason in Dei Filius.

faqs.question: Why did Pius IX call himself a prisoner of the Vatican?
faqs.answer: After the Kingdom of Italy captured Rome in 1870, he refused to recognize the annexation and never left the Vatican again. The standoff lasted until the Lateran Treaty of 1929.

faqs.question: What is Pius IX's connection to the United States?
faqs.answer: He approved the U.S. bishops' choice of Mary under the title of the Immaculate Conception as patroness of the nation and founded the Pontifical North American College in Rome in 1859.

directAnswer: Pope Leo XIII was Gioacchino Pecci, who reigned from 20 February 1878 to 20 July 1903 and died at 93, the oldest verified pope in office. He is the father of modern Catholic social teaching through the 1891 encyclical Rerum novarum, revived the study of St. Thomas Aquinas, wrote a series of encyclicals on the Rosary, and gave the Church the Prayer to St. Michael.

sections.h2: Gioacchino Pecci, Nuncio and Bishop of Perugia
paras: Gioacchino Vincenzo Pecci was born on 2 March 1810 in Carpineto Romano, south of Rome, at a time when the region was under Napoleonic rule. Educated by the Jesuits and at the Academy of Noble Ecclesiastics, he served as a papal governor of Benevento and Perugia and, in 1843, as nuncio to Belgium, where he observed industrial society and parliamentary politics firsthand.

From 1846 to 1877 he was bishop of Perugia, where he founded an academy devoted to St. Thomas Aquinas and wrote pastoral letters on the Church and modern civilization. Pius IX made him a cardinal in 1853 and, shortly before his death, camerlengo. Pecci was elected in February 1878 at nearly 68, and many expected a short, transitional reign.

sections.h2: Aeterni Patris and the Thomistic Revival
paras: In his 1879 encyclical Aeterni Patris Leo XIII urged that philosophy in Catholic schools and seminaries be grounded in the thought of St. Thomas Aquinas. He commissioned the critical Leonine edition of Aquinas's works, which continues today, and promoted Catholic scholarship more broadly. In 1881 he opened the Vatican Archives to scholars, saying the Church had nothing to fear from historical truth.
He also made John Henry Newman a cardinal in 1879, a gesture widely seen as recognition of serious Catholic thought in the English-speaking world.

sections.h2: Rerum novarum and the Condition of Workers
paras: On 15 May 1891 Leo XIII issued Rerum novarum, on capital and labor. Responding to the hardships of industrial workers, he rejected socialism and defended private property, while insisting that employers owe workers a just wage sufficient to support them, that the state has a duty to protect the weak, and that workers have the right to form associations. The encyclical became the foundation of modern Catholic social teaching, and later popes marked its anniversaries with their own social documents.

In 1896 he issued Apostolicae curae, declaring Anglican ordinations invalid. He also improved relations with Germany, helping to end the Kulturkampf, and urged French Catholics to accept the Republic.

sections.h2: Leo XIII and the Church in America
paras: Leo XIII took a close interest in the United States. He approved the founding of the Catholic University of America in Washington and in 1893 established an apostolic delegation there. In 1899 he addressed the letter Testem benevolentiae to Cardinal James Gibbons of Baltimore, cautioning against a set of ideas labeled Americanism, such as adapting doctrine to modern culture, while making clear he was not condemning the legitimate customs of the American nation.

sections.h2: The Pope of the Rosary and St. Michael
paras: Beginning in 1883 Leo XIII wrote about a dozen encyclicals on the Rosary and dedicated the month of October to it. He composed the Prayer to St. Michael the Archangel, which in 1886 was added to the prayers recited after Low Mass, and in 1899 consecrated the human race to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. He also approved new scapulars and encouraged devotion to the Holy Family and St. Joseph, notably in the 1889 encyclical Quamquam pluries.

He was the first pope to be filmed with a motion picture camera and the first whose voice was recorded. He died in July 1903 at 93, after more than 25 years as pope, and is buried in the Lateran basilica.

keyFacts: Born Gioacchino Pecci in Carpineto Romano on 2 March 1810
Reigned 20 February 1878 – 20 July 1903
Issued Rerum novarum on capital and labor (15 May 1891)
Promoted the study of Aquinas in Aeterni Patris (1879)
Wrote about a dozen Rosary encyclicals and composed the Prayer to St. Michael
Addressed Testem benevolentiae to Cardinal Gibbons (1899)

faqs.question: Why is Rerum novarum so important?
faqs.answer: Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical addressed the rights and duties of capital and labor, defending private property while affirming just wages, workers' associations and the state's duty to protect the poor. It launched the tradition of modern Catholic social teaching.

faqs.question: Did Leo XIII write the Prayer to St. Michael?
faqs.answer: Yes. Leo XIII composed the prayer, and in 1886 it was added to the prayers said after Low Mass. Many parishes have restored it in recent decades.

faqs.question: What was 'Americanism' in Leo XIII's letter?
faqs.answer: In Testem benevolentiae (1899) he warned against tendencies to adapt doctrine to modern culture or to downplay religious vows and spiritual direction, while stating he did not mean to criticize American political institutions or customs.

directAnswer: Pope St. Pius X was Giuseppe Sarto, a parish priest from the Veneto who rose to patriarch of Venice and reigned from 4 August 1903 to 20 August 1914. Under the motto 'to restore all things in Christ,' he opened frequent Communion to the faithful and early Communion to children, opposed Modernism, renewed sacred music, and began the codification of canon law. He was canonized in 1954.

sections.h2: Giuseppe Sarto, Parish Priest and Patriarch
paras: Giuseppe Melchiorre Sarto was born on 2 June 1835 in Riese, a village in the Veneto then ruled by Austria, the son of a postman and a seamstress. He studied at the seminary of Padua on a scholarship and was ordained in 1858. Unlike most modern popes, he spent years in ordinary parish ministry as a curate at Tombolo and pastor of Salzano, before serving as spiritual director of the Treviso seminary.

Leo XIII appointed him bishop of Mantua in 1884 and in 1893 cardinal and patriarch of Venice. In the 1903 conclave, after the emperor of Austria-Hungary exercised a claimed veto against Cardinal Rampolla, Sarto was elected. One of his first acts was to abolish any such secular veto in papal elections.

sections.h2: The Pope of the Eucharist
paras: Pius X's best-known reforms concern Holy Communion. The 1905 decree Sacra Tridentina Synodus encouraged frequent and even daily Communion for all who are in a state of grace and have a right intention, overturning lingering Jansenist rigor. The 1910 decree Quam singulari lowered the age of First Communion to the age of reason, around seven, rather than twelve or fourteen.
These changes transformed Catholic parish life worldwide, including in the United States, where generations of children have made First Communion in second grade because of his decree.

sections.h2: Gregorian Chant, the Breviary and Canon Law
paras: In his 1903 motu proprio Tra le sollecitudini Pius X called for the restoration of Gregorian chant and encouraged the active participation of the faithful in the liturgy. He also authorized a new official edition of the chant books and, in 1911, reformed the Roman Breviary, restoring the weekly recitation of the full Psalter.

In 1904 he launched the codification of the Church's canon law, entrusting it to Cardinal Pietro Gasparri; the resulting Code was promulgated in 1917 under Benedict XV. He reorganized the Roman Curia in 1908 and encouraged catechesis, and a catechism associated with his name was widely used.

sections.h2: The Campaign Against Modernism
paras: Pius X saw in Modernism, a movement that reinterpreted dogma and Scripture through historical and philosophical theories detached from Church teaching, the gravest threat of his day. In 1907 the Holy Office issued the decree Lamentabili, and the pope published the encyclical Pascendi Dominici gregis, calling Modernism the synthesis of all heresies. In 1910 he required clergy to take an Oath Against Modernism.
The campaign was effective in defending doctrine but also led to an atmosphere of suspicion in which some scholars were unjustly accused, a point historians frequently note.

sections.h2: Death, Canonization and Feast Day
paras: Pius X died on 20 August 1914, weeks after the outbreak of World War I, which he had tried to avert and which grieved him deeply. Known for his simplicity and charity, he was beatified by Pius XII in 1951 and canonized on 29 May 1954, the first pope canonized since Pius V in 1712. His memorial is celebrated on August 21, and his body rests in St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Giuseppe Sarto in Riese, Veneto, on 2 June 1835
Reigned 4 August 1903 – 20 August 1914
Motto: Instaurare omnia in Christo (To restore all things in Christ)
Encouraged frequent Communion (1905) and lowered First Communion age (1910)
Condemned Modernism in Pascendi (1907) and instituted the anti-Modernist oath (1910)
Canonized by Pius XII on 29 May 1954; memorial August 21

faqs.question: Why is St. Pius X called the Pope of the Eucharist?
faqs.answer: He encouraged frequent and daily Communion in 1905 and in 1910 allowed children to receive First Communion at the age of reason, around seven, changes that reshaped Catholic devotional life.

faqs.question: What was the Oath Against Modernism?
faqs.answer: Introduced by Pius X in 1910, it required clergy and teachers of theology to affirm key Catholic doctrines and reject Modernist errors. It remained in use until 1967.

faqs.question: When is the feast of St. Pius X?
faqs.answer: His memorial is celebrated on August 21. He was canonized in 1954, the first pope declared a saint since Pius V.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict XV was Giacomo della Chiesa of Genoa, elected weeks after World War I began, who reigned from 3 September 1914 to 22 January 1922. He labored for peace and for war victims, proposed a peace plan in 1917, promulgated the first Code of Canon Law, and renewed Catholic missionary strategy in Maximum illud.

sections.h2: A Diplomat from Genoa
paras: Giacomo Paolo Giovanni Battista della Chiesa was born in Genoa on 21 November 1854 to a noble family. He earned a law degree before entering the priesthood and trained in Church diplomacy. For years he worked closely with Cardinal Mariano Rampolla, secretary of state under Leo XIII, and later served as undersecretary of state.

In 1907 Pius X appointed him archbishop of Bologna, but he was made a cardinal only in May 1914. Just four months later, with Europe at war, the cardinals elected him pope, valuing his diplomatic experience.

sections.h2: Peace Efforts During the Great War
paras: Benedict XV kept the Holy See strictly neutral and repeatedly called the war the suicide of civilized Europe. His first encyclical, Ad beatissimi Apostolorum (1914), pleaded for an end to the fighting. On 1 August 1917 he sent the warring powers a peace note proposing disarmament, arbitration, freedom of the seas and the mutual renunciation of indemnities, but it was largely rejected by both sides.

He also organized extensive humanitarian relief: a Vatican office helped trace prisoners of war and missing soldiers, arranged exchanges of wounded prisoners, and supplied aid to civilians, draining the Holy See's finances. Benedict XVI, explaining his own choice of name in 2005, recalled him as a courageous prophet of peace.

sections.h2: The 1917 Code of Canon Law
paras: On Pentecost 1917 Benedict XV promulgated the Code of Canon Law, completing the project begun by Pius X under Cardinal Pietro Gasparri. For the first time the Latin Church's law was gathered into a single systematic code, which took effect in 1918 and remained in force until the revised Code of 1983.
In 1917 he also created the Congregation for the Eastern Church and founded the Pontifical Oriental Institute in Rome to strengthen ties with Eastern Christians.

sections.h2: Maximum illud and the Missions
paras: In the apostolic letter Maximum illud (1919) Benedict XV urged missionaries to put the Gospel before national interests and insisted on the training of native clergy who could one day lead their own churches. The document is regarded as a turning point in modern missionary thinking, and Pope Francis marked its centenary with an Extraordinary Missionary Month in 2019.

Benedict canonized Joan of Arc in 1920 and improved relations with France and Italy after the war. He also consecrated Eugenio Pacelli, the future Pius XII, as a bishop in May 1917. He died of pneumonia in January 1922 at 67.

keyFacts: Born Giacomo della Chiesa in Genoa on 21 November 1854
Reigned 3 September 1914 – 22 January 1922
Issued a peace proposal to the warring powers on 1 August 1917
Promulgated the first Code of Canon Law (1917)
Issued Maximum illud on the missions (1919)
Canonized St. Joan of Arc (1920)

faqs.question: What was Benedict XV's 1917 peace note?
faqs.answer: It was a proposal sent to the warring nations calling for disarmament, international arbitration, freedom of the seas and mutual renunciation of war indemnities. Both sides largely ignored it.

faqs.question: Why did Benedict XVI choose the name Benedict partly because of Benedict XV?
faqs.answer: In 2005 Benedict XVI said he wished to follow Benedict XV, whom he praised as a courageous prophet of peace who guided the Church through World War I, as well as St. Benedict of Nursia.

faqs.question: What did Maximum illud change?
faqs.answer: Benedict XV's 1919 letter told missionaries not to serve their own nations' interests and stressed forming local clergy, shaping the Church's missionary approach for the rest of the century.

directAnswer: Pope Pius XI was Achille Ratti, a scholar-librarian and mountaineer from Lombardy who reigned from 6 February 1922 to 10 February 1939. He signed the Lateran Treaty that created Vatican City, instituted the feast of Christ the King, issued the social encyclical Quadragesimo anno, founded Vatican Radio, and condemned both Nazism and Communism.

sections.h2: Librarian, Alpinist and Nuncio to Poland
paras: Achille Ratti was born on 31 May 1857 in Desio, near Milan, the son of a silk-factory manager. Ordained in 1879, he spent most of his career as a scholar, first at Milan's Ambrosian Library, which he eventually directed, and from 1911 at the Vatican Library, where he became prefect. He was also an accomplished mountaineer who made notable ascents in the Alps.

In 1918 Benedict XV sent him to Poland, first as apostolic visitor and then as nuncio, and he remained in Warsaw during the Soviet advance of 1920. In 1921 he was named archbishop of Milan and a cardinal, and only months later was elected pope, taking as his motto the peace of Christ in the kingdom of Christ.

sections.h2: The Lateran Treaty and Vatican City
paras: Pius XI resolved the Roman Question that had divided the papacy and Italy since 1870. On 11 February 1929 his representatives signed the Lateran Pacts with the Italian government: a treaty recognizing the sovereignty of the Holy See over the new State of Vatican City, a financial settlement, and a concordat regulating the Church's position in Italy.

The pope then left the Vatican and appeared in public in Rome, ending the long self-imposed seclusion of his predecessors. In 1931 he inaugurated Vatican Radio, built with Guglielmo Marconi, and in 1936 he refounded the Pontifical Academy of Sciences.

sections.h2: Christ the King, Marriage and Quadragesimo anno
paras: In the 1925 encyclical Quas primas Pius XI instituted the feast of Christ the King, presenting Christ's kingship as the answer to secularism and aggressive nationalism. His 1930 encyclical Casti connubii taught on Christian marriage, reaffirming its indissolubility and condemning artificial contraception.

For the fortieth anniversary of Rerum novarum he issued Quadragesimo anno (1931), developing Catholic social teaching and articulating the principle of subsidiarity: higher authorities should not take over what smaller communities can do for themselves. He also gave strong support to Catholic Action, the organized apostolate of the laity.

sections.h2: Against Totalitarianism: Mit brennender Sorge and Divini Redemptoris
paras: Pius XI faced the rise of totalitarian regimes. He condemned the persecution of the Church in Mexico and in Soviet Russia, and in 1931 he protested Mussolini's moves against Catholic Action. In March 1937 he issued Mit brennender Sorge, written in German and smuggled into Germany to be read from pulpits, denouncing Nazi violations of the 1933 concordat and its racial and neo-pagan ideology.

Days later, in Divini Redemptoris, he condemned atheistic Communism. In his final years he spoke out against racism and antisemitism, and at his death in February 1939 he was preparing further statements on these themes.

sections.h2: Saints of the Interwar Church
paras: Pius XI canonized many saints whose devotion remains strong among American Catholics, including Thérèse of Lisieux in 1925, John Vianney in 1925, John Bosco in 1934, and Thomas More and John Fisher in 1935. He named Thérèse patroness of the missions. He is buried in the grottoes of St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Achille Ratti in Desio, Lombardy, on 31 May 1857
Reigned 6 February 1922 – 10 February 1939
Signed the Lateran Treaty creating Vatican City (11 February 1929)
Instituted the feast of Christ the King in Quas primas (1925)
Issued Quadragesimo anno (1931) and Mit brennender Sorge (1937)
Inaugurated Vatican Radio (1931)

faqs.question: What did the Lateran Treaty accomplish?
faqs.answer: Signed in 1929 under Pius XI, it created the sovereign State of Vatican City, settled the dispute with Italy over the loss of the Papal States, and included a concordat on the Church's status in Italy.

faqs.question: Why did Pius XI institute the feast of Christ the King?
