faqs.answer: In Quas primas (1925) he established the feast to proclaim Christ's authority over individuals and societies in response to rising secularism and nationalism. Today it is celebrated on the last Sunday of the liturgical year.

faqs.question: What was Mit brennender Sorge?
faqs.answer: It was Pius XI's 1937 encyclical in German, secretly distributed and read in German churches, condemning Nazi violations of the concordat and its racist, neo-pagan ideology.

directAnswer: Venerable Pius XII was Eugenio Pacelli, a Roman-born Vatican diplomat who reigned from 2 March 1939 to 9 October 1958, guiding the Church through World War II and the early Cold War. He defined the dogma of Mary's Assumption in 1950, issued major encyclicals on the Church, Scripture and liturgy, and remains debated for his response to the Holocaust. He was declared Venerable in 2009.

sections.h2: A Roman Diplomat: Munich, Berlin and the Secretariat of State
paras: Eugenio Maria Giuseppe Giovanni Pacelli was born in Rome on 2 March 1876 into a family long connected with papal service, the first pope born after the unification of Italy. Ordained in 1899, he joined the Secretariat of State and worked with Cardinal Gasparri on the codification of canon law.

In 1917 Benedict XV consecrated him archbishop and sent him as nuncio to Bavaria, and later to the German Republic, where he negotiated concordats. Pius XI made him a cardinal and, in 1930, secretary of state; in that role he signed the 1933 concordat with Germany and in 1936 made an extensive visit to the United States. He was elected on his sixty-third birthday in one of the shortest conclaves of modern times.

sections.h2: World War II and the Holocaust Debate
paras: Pius XII tried to prevent the war and then kept the Holy See formally neutral. The Vatican ran an information office for prisoners and refugees, and during the German occupation of Rome in 1943–1944 many Jews and others found shelter in Church institutions, including religious houses and Vatican properties. His 1942 Christmas message spoke of hundreds of thousands of people condemned to death or slow decline, sometimes only because of their nationality or race.

Critics argue that he should have condemned the Nazi extermination of the Jews more explicitly and by name; defenders argue that public protest would have provoked worse reprisals and that quiet aid saved many lives. The opening of the Vatican archives for his pontificate in 2020 has given historians new material, and the debate continues.

sections.h2: Munificentissimus Deus and the Assumption
paras: On 1 November 1950, after consulting the world's bishops, Pius XII solemnly defined in the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus that the Immaculate Mother of God, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory. It is the only time a pope has invoked the infallibility defined at Vatican I since that council.
He consecrated the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary in 1942, proclaimed a Marian Year in 1954, and in the same year instituted the feast of the Queenship of Mary.

sections.h2: Encyclicals on the Church, Scripture and Liturgy
paras: His teaching was voluminous. Mystici Corporis (1943) presented the Church as the Mystical Body of Christ. Divino afflante Spiritu (1943) encouraged Catholic biblical scholars to study the original languages and literary forms of Scripture. Mediator Dei (1947) addressed the liturgy and the participation of the faithful, and Humani generis (1950) warned against theological errors while allowing that the bodily origin of the human person through evolution could be studied, provided the soul is held to be directly created by God.
In practice, he restored the Easter Vigil, reformed the rites of Holy Week in 1955, and relaxed the Eucharistic fast, allowing evening Masses. He also internationalized the College of Cardinals.

sections.h2: Death and the Cause for Beatification
paras: Pius XII died at Castel Gandolfo on 9 October 1958. Pope Benedict XVI declared him Venerable on 19 December 2009, recognizing his heroic virtue. Beatification would require an approved miracle, and his cause remains open.

keyFacts: Born Eugenio Pacelli in Rome on 2 March 1876
Reigned 2 March 1939 – 9 October 1958
Nuncio to Bavaria and Germany; secretary of state under Pius XI
Defined the Assumption in Munificentissimus Deus (1 November 1950)
Issued Mystici Corporis, Divino afflante Spiritu, Mediator Dei and Humani generis
Declared Venerable by Benedict XVI on 19 December 2009

faqs.question: Why is Pius XII's response to the Holocaust controversial?
faqs.answer: He did not publicly condemn the Nazi genocide of the Jews by name. Critics see this as a moral failure; defenders point to the danger of reprisals and to sheltering and relief efforts that saved lives. Archives opened in 2020 are informing ongoing research.

faqs.question: What dogma did Pius XII define?
faqs.answer: In 1950 he defined the Assumption of Mary, teaching that at the end of her earthly life she was taken body and soul into heavenly glory. It is celebrated each year on August 15.

faqs.question: Why is Pius XII called Venerable?
faqs.answer: Benedict XVI recognized his heroic virtue in 2009, giving him the title Venerable. His beatification would require a verified miracle attributed to his intercession.

directAnswer: Pope St. John XXIII was Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli, a farmer's son from near Bergamo who reigned from 28 October 1958 to 3 June 1963. Elected at nearly 77 and expected to be a caretaker, he convoked the Second Vatican Council, issued the encyclicals Mater et magistra and Pacem in terris, and was canonized in 2014. Catholics remember him as Good Pope John.

sections.h2: Angelo Roncalli of Sotto il Monte
paras: Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was born on 25 November 1881 in Sotto il Monte, a village near Bergamo, the fourth of thirteen children in a family of sharecroppers. Ordained in 1904, he served as secretary to the bishop of Bergamo, taught Church history, and was a medical orderly and chaplain in the Italian army during World War I.

He was also a historian of note, editing the records of St. Charles Borromeo's visitation of Bergamo. His spiritual journal, published after his death as Journal of a Soul, shows a steady, simple piety sustained over decades.

sections.h2: Diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and France
paras: In 1925 Roncalli was made a bishop and sent to Bulgaria as apostolic visitor, then delegate. From 1935 he served as apostolic delegate to Turkey and Greece, based in Istanbul, where he built relations with the Orthodox and with Muslim authorities. During World War II he is credited with helping Jewish refugees obtain documents and safe passage, efforts later recognized by Jewish organizations.
In 1944 Pius XII sent him as nuncio to newly liberated France. In 1953 he became cardinal and patriarch of Venice, where he expected to end his ministry as a pastor.

sections.h2: Convoking the Second Vatican Council
paras: Elected in October 1958 at nearly 77, Roncalli took the name John. On 25 January 1959, at the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls, he announced his intention to hold an ecumenical council, along with a Roman synod and a revision of canon law. He spoke of aggiornamento, bringing the Church up to date so that it could present the unchanging Gospel more effectively to the modern world.

After years of preparation, he opened the Second Vatican Council on 11 October 1962. He also established the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity in 1960, invited non-Catholic observers to the council, and in 1962 added the name of St. Joseph to the Roman Canon of the Mass.

sections.h2: Mater et magistra and Pacem in terris
paras: In Mater et magistra (1961) John XXIII applied Catholic social teaching to modern conditions, including agriculture and the relations between rich and poor nations. During the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962 he made a public radio appeal for peace that was reported to have been welcomed in both Washington and Moscow.

His last encyclical, Pacem in terris (April 1963), addressed not only to Catholics but to all people of good will, set out the foundations of peace in human rights and duties and called for an end to the arms race. It was widely read beyond the Church.

sections.h2: Good Pope John's Death and Canonization
paras: John XXIII died of stomach cancer on 3 June 1963, between the council's first and second sessions, mourned around the world. John Paul II beatified him on 3 September 2000, and Pope Francis canonized him on 27 April 2014 together with John Paul II. His memorial is celebrated on October 11, the anniversary of the council's opening, and his body lies in St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli in Sotto il Monte on 25 November 1881
Reigned 28 October 1958 – 3 June 1963
Announced the Second Vatican Council on 25 January 1959; opened it 11 October 1962
Issued Mater et magistra (1961) and Pacem in terris (1963)
Canonized by Pope Francis on 27 April 2014; memorial October 11
Motto: Obedientia et pax (Obedience and peace)

faqs.question: Why did John XXIII call the Second Vatican Council?
faqs.answer: He wanted the Church to renew itself and present the Gospel more effectively in the modern world, a goal he described as aggiornamento. He announced the council in January 1959, only three months after his election.

faqs.question: What is Pacem in terris about?
faqs.answer: Issued in April 1963 and addressed to all people of good will, it grounds world peace in respect for human rights and duties, the common good and the rule of law, and urges an end to the nuclear arms race.

faqs.question: Why is his feast day October 11 rather than the day he died?
faqs.answer: The Church chose October 11, the anniversary of his opening of the Second Vatican Council in 1962, as his memorial.

directAnswer: Pope St. Paul VI was Giovanni Battista Montini, former archbishop of Milan, who reigned from 21 June 1963 to 6 August 1978. He guided the Second Vatican Council to its close, carried out its liturgical reform, traveled to six continents, lifted the 1054 excommunications with Constantinople, and issued Humanae vitae. He was canonized in 2018.

sections.h2: Giovanni Battista Montini, Servant of the Secretariat of State
paras: Giovanni Battista Montini was born on 26 September 1897 in Concesio, near Brescia, the son of a lawyer and Catholic journalist active in politics. Frail as a youth, he was ordained in 1920 and soon entered the Vatican's diplomatic service. He spent three decades in the Secretariat of State, working closely with Pius XII and serving as substitute, and was also chaplain to Italian Catholic university students.

In 1954 Pius XII named him archbishop of Milan, where he devoted himself to reaching industrial workers and organized a large city mission. John XXIII made him the first cardinal of his pontificate in 1958, and Montini was elected pope in June 1963, taking the name of the Apostle Paul.

sections.h2: Bringing Vatican II to Completion
paras: Paul VI reconvened the Second Vatican Council and presided over its last three sessions, promulgating its sixteen documents, including the constitutions on the liturgy, on the Church, on divine revelation, and on the Church in the modern world. He closed the council on 8 December 1965.

He then implemented it. He created the Synod of Bishops in 1965, reformed the Roman Curia, and promulgated the revised Roman Missal in 1969, which introduced the form of the Mass now celebrated in parishes, increasingly in the vernacular. He was also the last pope to be crowned with the papal tiara, which he later gave away, and it is now displayed at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington, D.C.

sections.h2: The Pilgrim Pope and the Sister Churches
paras: In January 1964 Paul VI made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, the first papal journey outside Italy in more than 150 years, and met Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I in Jerusalem. On 7 December 1965 the two simultaneously lifted the mutual excommunications of 1054. In 1967 he visited the patriarch in Istanbul.

He traveled to India, to Colombia, to Uganda, where he honored the Ugandan martyrs he had canonized, and to Asia and Oceania. In October 1965 he addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York, pleading for an end to war, and celebrated Mass at Yankee Stadium during that visit.

sections.h2: Humanae vitae, Populorum progressio and Evangelii nuntiandi
paras: Paul VI's 1967 encyclical Populorum progressio addressed global development and the duties of wealthy nations toward poorer ones. In July 1968 he issued Humanae vitae, which reaffirmed that each marital act must remain open to the transmission of life and rejected artificial contraception. The encyclical met strong dissent in some quarters, and the pope wrote no further encyclicals afterward.

In 1968 he also proclaimed the Credo of the People of God, and in 1975 he issued the apostolic exhortation Evangelii nuntiandi on evangelization in the modern world, a text frequently cited by his successors.

sections.h2: Death on the Transfiguration and Canonization
paras: Paul VI died at Castel Gandolfo on 6 August 1978, the feast of the Transfiguration. Pope Francis beatified him on 19 October 2014 and canonized him on 14 October 2018, alongside St. Oscar Romero. His optional memorial is kept on May 29, the anniversary of his priestly ordination.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Battista Montini in Concesio on 26 September 1897
Reigned 21 June 1963 – 6 August 1978
Closed the Second Vatican Council on 8 December 1965
Lifted the 1054 excommunications with Patriarch Athenagoras I (1965)
Issued Populorum progressio (1967) and Humanae vitae (1968)
Canonized by Pope Francis on 14 October 2018; memorial May 29

faqs.question: What did Humanae vitae teach?
faqs.answer: Issued by Paul VI in 1968, Humanae vitae reaffirmed that the unitive and procreative meanings of marriage are inseparable and that artificial contraception is morally wrong, while approving natural methods of spacing births for serious reasons.

faqs.question: Where is Paul VI's papal tiara today?
faqs.answer: Paul VI gave up the tiara after his coronation as a gesture of solidarity with the poor. It was later given to the Catholic Church in the United States and is displayed at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington, D.C.

faqs.question: What happened between Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras?
faqs.answer: They met in Jerusalem in 1964, the first meeting of a pope and an ecumenical patriarch in centuries, and on 7 December 1965 they jointly lifted the mutual excommunications of 1054.

directAnswer: Pope John Paul I was Albino Luciani, patriarch of Venice, who reigned for only 33 days, from 26 August to 28 September 1978. The first pope to take a double name, honoring John XXIII and Paul VI, he replaced the papal coronation with a simpler inauguration Mass and won affection with his warmth and smile. He was beatified in 2022.

sections.h2: Albino Luciani of the Dolomites
paras: Albino Luciani was born on 17 October 1912 in Forno di Canale, now Canale d'Agordo, a mountain village in the Veneto, to a poor family; his father was a seasonal worker who had labored abroad. Ordained in 1935, he taught in the seminary of Belluno, earned a doctorate in theology, and served as vicar general of his diocese. He was the first pope born in the twentieth century.

John XXIII made him bishop of Vittorio Veneto in 1958. He attended all sessions of the Second Vatican Council, and Paul VI named him patriarch of Venice in 1969 and a cardinal in 1973. In Venice he became known for his simple style and his catechetical gifts.

sections.h2: Illustrissimi and a Gift for Teaching
paras: While patriarch, Luciani wrote a series of imaginative open letters for a Catholic magazine, addressed to figures such as Charles Dickens, Mark Twain, Pinocchio and St. Bernard. Collected in the book Illustrissimi, they show his ability to explain the faith in a light, accessible way.

As pope he continued that style in his Wednesday audiences, speaking plainly about faith, hope and charity, sometimes inviting children to speak with him. His episcopal motto, Humilitas, summarized his manner.

sections.h2: Thirty-Three Days as Pope
paras: Elected on 26 August 1978 on the second day of the conclave, Luciani took the name John Paul in honor of his two immediate predecessors, the first double name in papal history, and the first to add 'the First.' He declined a coronation and instead began his ministry with a Mass of inauguration on 3 September 1978, a practice his successors have kept.

On the morning of 28 September 1978 he was found dead in his bed. The Vatican attributed his death to a heart attack. His sudden death gave rise to speculation, but the conclusions of the investigation for his beatification support death from natural causes. He was the most recent Italian pope.

sections.h2: Beatification of the Smiling Pope
paras: After a miracle attributed to his intercession was approved, Pope Francis beatified John Paul I in St. Peter's Square on 4 September 2022. He is buried in the grottoes beneath St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Born Albino Luciani in Forno di Canale (Canale d'Agordo) on 17 October 1912
Reigned 26 August 1978 – 28 September 1978 (33 days)
Patriarch of Venice from 1969; cardinal from 1973
First pope with a double name; replaced the coronation with an inauguration Mass
Author of Illustrissimi, letters to historical and fictional figures
Beatified by Pope Francis on 4 September 2022

faqs.question: Why did John Paul I choose a double name?
faqs.answer: He chose John Paul to honor both John XXIII, who made him a bishop, and Paul VI, who made him patriarch of Venice and a cardinal, signaling continuity with the Second Vatican Council.

faqs.question: How did John Paul I die?
faqs.answer: He was found dead on 28 September 1978, 33 days after his election. The Vatican attributed his death to a heart attack, and the research for his beatification concluded he died of natural causes.

faqs.question: Is John Paul I a saint?
faqs.answer: He has been beatified, which allows him to be called Blessed. Pope Francis beatified him on 4 September 2022 after approving a miracle attributed to his intercession.

directAnswer: Pope St. John Paul II was Karol Wojtyła of Poland, the first non-Italian pope in 455 years, who reigned from 16 October 1978 to 2 April 2005, one of the longest pontificates in history. He traveled to more than 120 countries, helped inspire the peaceful end of communism in Eastern Europe, founded World Youth Day, promulgated the Catechism of the Catholic Church, and was canonized in 2014.

sections.h2: Karol Wojtyła: Actor, Laborer, Priest and Philosopher
paras: Karol Józef Wojtyła was born on 18 May 1920 in Wadowice, Poland. By the age of twenty he had lost his mother, his only brother and his father. During the Nazi occupation he worked in a quarry and a chemical plant, took part in an underground theater, and studied for the priesthood in a clandestine seminary in Kraków. He was ordained in 1946.

After doctoral studies in Rome and Poland he taught ethics at the Catholic University of Lublin and developed a philosophy of the human person. He became auxiliary bishop of Kraków in 1958, participated in the Second Vatican Council, and was named archbishop of Kraków in 1964 and a cardinal in 1967.

sections.h2: A Polish Pope and the Fall of Communism
paras: Elected on 16 October 1978 at 58, he was the first Polish pope and the first non-Italian since Adrian VI. His inaugural homily urged the world, Be not afraid. His first visit to Poland in June 1979 drew enormous crowds and is widely credited with helping to give rise to the Solidarity movement.

On 13 May 1981 he was shot in St. Peter's Square by Mehmet Ali Ağca and seriously wounded. He attributed his survival to Our Lady of Fatima, whose feast falls on that day, and later visited and forgave his attacker in prison. Historians broadly agree that his moral support for freedom in Poland contributed to the largely peaceful collapse of communist regimes in 1989.

sections.h2: Teaching: Encyclicals, the Catechism and the Theology of the Body
paras: John Paul II wrote fourteen encyclicals, among them Redemptor hominis (1979), Laborem exercens (1981), Centesimus annus (1991), Veritatis splendor (1993), Evangelium vitae (1995), in which he urged a culture of life, and Fides et ratio (1998). His Wednesday catechesis from 1979 to 1984 on human love became known as the Theology of the Body.

He promulgated the revised Code of Canon Law in 1983 and the Catechism of the Catholic Church in 1992. In 2002 he added the Luminous Mysteries to the Rosary, and in 2000 he established Divine Mercy Sunday for the universal Church.

sections.h2: World Youth Day and the Pilgrim Pope in America
paras: He made more than a hundred journeys abroad, visiting the United States several times, including his 1979 tour and his 1987 visit, and in 1993 he celebrated World Youth Day in Denver. He had established World Youth Day in the mid-1980s, and the gatherings drew millions of young people.

He also pursued dialogue with other Christians and other religions: he visited the synagogue of Rome in 1986, convened the World Day of Prayer for Peace in Assisi that year, and prayed at the Western Wall in Jerusalem during the Great Jubilee of 2000. He canonized and beatified more people than any earlier pope.

sections.h2: Suffering, Death and Canonization
paras: In his later years he lived publicly with Parkinson's disease, continuing his ministry as his strength declined. He died on 2 April 2005, the vigil of Divine Mercy Sunday. Benedict XVI beatified him on 1 May 2011, and Pope Francis canonized him on 27 April 2014. His memorial is celebrated on October 22, the anniversary of his papal inauguration.

keyFacts: Born Karol Wojtyła in Wadowice, Poland, on 18 May 1920
Reigned 16 October 1978 – 2 April 2005
Survived an assassination attempt on 13 May 1981
Promulgated the 1983 Code of Canon Law and the 1992 Catechism
Established World Youth Day; hosted WYD Denver 1993
Canonized by Pope Francis on 27 April 2014; memorial October 22

faqs.question: What is the Theology of the Body?
faqs.answer: It is the name given to John Paul II's series of Wednesday audiences from 1979 to 1984 on the meaning of the human body, sexuality and marriage in God's plan, which has strongly influenced Catholic marriage preparation and catechesis.

faqs.question: How did John Paul II contribute to the fall of communism?
faqs.answer: His 1979 pilgrimage to Poland and steady defense of human rights and religious freedom encouraged the Solidarity movement and peaceful resistance, which historians see as a factor in the collapse of communist rule in 1989.

faqs.question: Why is his feast day October 22?
faqs.answer: October 22 is the anniversary of his papal inauguration Mass in 1978, at which he told the world, Be not afraid. The Church chose it for his memorial after his canonization in 2014.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict XVI was Joseph Ratzinger, a German theologian and longtime head of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, who reigned from 19 April 2005 until his resignation on 28 February 2013. He wrote the encyclicals Deus caritas est, Spe salvi and Caritas in veritate, the Jesus of Nazareth trilogy, widened use of the traditional Latin Mass, and became the first pope to resign freely in nearly 600 years.

sections.h2: Joseph Ratzinger: Bavarian Theologian at Vatican II
paras: Joseph Aloisius Ratzinger was born on 16 April 1927 in Marktl, Bavaria, the son of a police officer. As a teenager he was conscripted into wartime auxiliary service, and after the war he studied for the priesthood with his brother Georg; both were ordained in 1951.

He became one of the leading theologians of his generation, teaching at Bonn, Münster, Tübingen and Regensburg. At the Second Vatican Council he served as theological adviser to Cardinal Joseph Frings of Cologne. His book Introduction to Christianity (1968) remains widely read.

sections.h2: Archbishop of Munich and Prefect for the Doctrine of the Faith
paras: Paul VI appointed him archbishop of Munich and Freising and made him a cardinal in 1977. In 1981 John Paul II called him to Rome as prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, a post he held for nearly 24 years. He oversaw the preparation of the Catechism of the Catholic Church and became one of John Paul II's closest collaborators.

As dean of the College of Cardinals he presided at John Paul II's funeral in April 2005. Days later, at 78, he was elected on the second day of the conclave and took the name Benedict, recalling both St. Benedict of Nursia, patron of Europe, and Benedict XV, the pope of peace during World War I.

sections.h2: Deus caritas est, Caritas in veritate and Jesus of Nazareth
paras: His first encyclical, Deus caritas est (2005), reflected on God as love and on the Church's charitable work. Spe salvi (2007) treated Christian hope, and Caritas in veritate (2009) applied social teaching to globalization and the economy, calling for ethics grounded in truth and charity. While pope he also published, as a private theologian, the three-volume Jesus of Nazareth.

In 2007 the motu proprio Summorum Pontificum allowed wider celebration of the Mass according to the 1962 Missal as an extraordinary form of the Roman Rite. In 2009 the apostolic constitution Anglicanorum coetibus created ordinariates allowing groups of former Anglicans to enter full communion while keeping elements of their heritage; the U.S. ordinariate was established in 2012.

sections.h2: Journeys, Regensburg and the Abuse Crisis
paras: In April 2008 Benedict XVI visited the United States, addressing the United Nations, celebrating Mass at Yankee Stadium and Nationals Park, and meeting privately with survivors of clerical sexual abuse. In 2010 he beatified John Henry Newman during a state visit to Britain. His 2006 Regensburg lecture on faith and reason provoked protests over a quotation about Islam, after which he expressed regret for the offense and pursued dialogue with Muslim leaders.

He strengthened procedures against abuse and laicized many offending priests, though critics argued the Church's response remained insufficient, particularly in his earlier years as archbishop and prefect.

sections.h2: Resignation and Life as Pope Emeritus
paras: On 11 February 2013 he announced in Latin that, owing to advanced age and declining strength, he would renounce the papacy, effective 28 February 2013. He was the first pope to resign since Gregory XII in 1415 and the first to do so on his own initiative since Celestine V in 1294. He lived as pope emeritus in a monastery in the Vatican gardens and died on 31 December 2022 at 95, among the longest-lived popes on record.

keyFacts: Born Joseph Ratzinger in Marktl, Bavaria, on 16 April 1927
Reigned 19 April 2005 – 28 February 2013
Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, 1981–2005
Wrote Deus caritas est (2005), Spe salvi (2007) and Caritas in veritate (2009)
Issued Summorum Pontificum (2007) and Anglicanorum coetibus (2009)
Resigned in 2013; died as pope emeritus on 31 December 2022

faqs.question: Why did Benedict XVI resign?
faqs.answer: He said that, because of advanced age, his strength of mind and body was no longer adequate to the demands of the papacy. He announced his decision on 11 February 2013, and it took effect on 28 February.

faqs.question: What did Summorum Pontificum allow?
faqs.answer: This 2007 document let priests celebrate Mass using the 1962 Roman Missal more freely, recognizing it as an extraordinary form of the Roman Rite alongside the ordinary form promulgated by Paul VI.

faqs.question: Did Benedict XVI visit the United States?
faqs.answer: Yes. In April 2008 he visited Washington and New York, addressed the United Nations, celebrated public Masses, prayed at Ground Zero, and met privately with abuse survivors.

directAnswer: Pope Francis was Jorge Mario Bergoglio, a Jesuit and archbishop of Buenos Aires who reigned from 13 March 2013 until his death on 21 April 2025. The first pope from the Americas, the first Jesuit pope and the first to take the name Francis, he emphasized mercy and care for the poor, wrote Laudato si' on care for creation, and led a multi-year Synod on synodality.

sections.h2: Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Buenos Aires
paras: Jorge Mario Bergoglio was born on 17 December 1936 in Buenos Aires, Argentina, the son of Italian immigrants. He trained as a chemical technician before entering the Society of Jesus in 1958, and was ordained a priest in 1969. He served as Jesuit provincial of Argentina from 1973 to 1979, during the years of military dictatorship, and later as rector of a Jesuit seminary.

John Paul II named him auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires in 1992, archbishop in 1998, and cardinal in 2001. As archbishop he was known for living in a simple apartment, using public transportation, and frequently visiting the city's poorest neighborhoods.

sections.h2: A Pope of Many Firsts
paras: Elected on 13 March 2013 after the resignation of Benedict XVI, he became the first pope from the Americas and the Southern Hemisphere, the first Jesuit pope, and the first non-European pope in well over a thousand years. He chose the name Francis after St. Francis of Assisi, as a sign of his concern for the poor, for peace and for creation.
He chose to live in the Casa Santa Marta guesthouse rather than the papal apartments. His motto, Miserando atque eligendo, comes from a homily of St. Bede on the call of St. Matthew.

sections.h2: Evangelii gaudium, Laudato si' and Fratelli tutti
paras: His apostolic exhortation Evangelii gaudium (2013) called the Church to missionary joy and to go out to the peripheries. The encyclical Laudato si' (2015) addressed care for our common home, linking environmental degradation, including climate change, to poverty and to a throwaway culture. Fratelli tutti (2020) reflected on human fraternity and social friendship, and Dilexit nos (2024) returned to devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

Amoris laetitia (2016), following two synods on the family, addressed marriage and family life, and its guidance on accompanying divorced and remarried Catholics generated considerable discussion. He proclaimed an Extraordinary Jubilee of Mercy in 2015–2016.

sections.h2: Reform, Synodality and Journeys
paras: Francis reorganized the Roman Curia with the apostolic constitution Praedicate Evangelium (2022) and appointed many cardinals from regions never before represented, giving the College a non-European majority. He convened a Synod on synodality that included lay voting members for the first time. His 2021 motu proprio Traditionis custodes placed new restrictions on the pre-conciliar Mass.

He traveled widely, including to the Arabian Peninsula in 2019, where he signed the Document on Human Fraternity in Abu Dhabi. In September 2015 he visited the United States, canonizing St. Junípero Serra in Washington and becoming the first pope to address a joint meeting of Congress, before attending the World Meeting of Families in Philadelphia.

sections.h2: Final Illness and Death on Easter Monday
paras: After a long hospitalization in early 2025, Francis appeared to bless the crowd on Easter Sunday and died the next morning, 21 April 2025, at 88, during the Jubilee Year he had opened. At his request he was buried in the Basilica of St. Mary Major in Rome rather than St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Born Jorge Mario Bergoglio in Buenos Aires on 17 December 1936
Reigned 13 March 2013 – 21 April 2025
First Jesuit pope and first pope from the Americas
Wrote Evangelii gaudium, Laudato si', Amoris laetitia and Fratelli tutti
First pope to address a joint meeting of the U.S. Congress (2015)
Buried in the Basilica of St. Mary Major, Rome

faqs.question: Why did Pope Francis choose the name Francis?
faqs.answer: He chose it in honor of St. Francis of Assisi, explaining soon after his election that the saint represented poverty, peace and care for creation, themes he wanted to define his pontificate.

faqs.question: What is Laudato si' about?
faqs.answer: Published in 2015, Laudato si' calls for care of our common home, connecting environmental problems such as pollution and climate change with poverty, consumerism and the dignity of every human life.

faqs.question: Where is Pope Francis buried?
faqs.answer: At his own request he was buried in the Basilica of St. Mary Major in Rome, a church he visited before and after nearly every papal journey to pray before the Marian icon Salus Populi Romani.

directAnswer: Pope Leo XIV is Robert Francis Prevost, a Chicago-born Augustinian friar who spent many years as a missionary and bishop in Peru, elected on 8 May 2025. He is the first pope born in the United States, the first from North America, and the first Augustinian pope. Before his election he led the worldwide Augustinian order and served as prefect of the Vatican's Dicastery for Bishops.

sections.h2: From the South Side of Chicago to the Augustinians
paras: Robert Francis Prevost was born on 14 September 1955 in Chicago and grew up in the south suburb of Dolton, Illinois, the son of a school administrator and a parish-active mother, with roots that include French, Italian, Spanish and Louisiana Creole ancestry. He studied mathematics at Villanova University, graduating in 1977, and entered the Order of St. Augustine that year.

He earned a Master of Divinity at Catholic Theological Union in Chicago and was ordained a priest in 1982. He then completed a doctorate in canon law at the Pontifical University of St. Thomas Aquinas in Rome.

sections.h2: Missionary and Bishop in Peru
paras: In 1985 Father Prevost was sent to the Augustinian mission in northern Peru, where over the following decade he served as a parish priest, seminary formator, teacher of canon law and judicial vicar, chiefly in the Archdiocese of Trujillo. He returned to Chicago as provincial of his order's Midwest province in 1999.

From 2001 to 2013 he served two terms as prior general of the Augustinians, based in Rome and visiting the order's communities around the world. In 2014 Pope Francis sent him back to Peru as apostolic administrator of the Diocese of Chiclayo, naming him its bishop in 2015; that year he also became a Peruvian citizen.

sections.h2: Prefect for Bishops and Election in 2025
paras: In January 2023 Francis called him to Rome as prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops, the office that helps the pope select bishops worldwide, and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America. He was created a cardinal in September 2023.

After the death of Francis, the conclave elected Prevost on 8 May 2025, on its second day. Appearing on the loggia of St. Peter's, he greeted the crowd with the words 'Peace be with you all' and spoke in Italian and Spanish. His papal inauguration Mass was celebrated on 18 May 2025.

sections.h2: Why the Name Leo
paras: Addressing the cardinals two days after his election, Leo XIV explained that he chose his name chiefly in reference to Leo XIII, whose encyclical Rerum novarum addressed the social question of the first Industrial Revolution. He said the Church must now respond to a new industrial revolution and to developments in artificial intelligence that raise fresh questions about human dignity, justice and labor.

His motto, In illo Uno unum, comes from St. Augustine and speaks of Christians being one in the one Christ, reflecting his Augustinian formation and emphasis on unity in the Church. He is the second pope from an English-speaking country, after the twelfth-century Englishman Adrian IV.

keyFacts: Born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago on 14 September 1955
Elected 8 May 2025; inaugurated 18 May 2025
First U.S.-born pope and first Augustinian pope
Missionary in Peru; bishop of Chiclayo; Peruvian citizen since 2015
Prior general of the Augustinians, 2001–2013
Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops from 2023

faqs.question: Why did Pope Leo XIV choose the name Leo?
faqs.answer: He said he chose it mainly to follow Leo XIII, author of Rerum novarum, because the Church faces a new industrial revolution and the challenges of artificial intelligence for human dignity, justice and work.

faqs.question: What is Pope Leo XIV's connection to Peru?
faqs.answer: He served as an Augustinian missionary in northern Peru beginning in 1985 and later as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023. He became a Peruvian citizen in 2015 and holds both U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.

faqs.question: Where did Pope Leo XIV go to college?
faqs.answer: He earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Villanova University in 1977, studied theology at Catholic Theological Union in Chicago, and received a doctorate in canon law from the Angelicum in Rome.
